Now, I should also double-check the assumption that "only boundary cells of runs and single-cell run cells change." The claim: an interface only eats its own two cells; once a cell hits 0, the interface dies and the next cell never participates. Is that really correct? An interface between cell x (boundary of run R1) and y (boundary of run R2): while x>0>y: x -= 1, y += 1. x can only become 0 (it starts positive, decreases by 1 per step: reaches 0 and stops — at that point the interface is dead, so x never decreases below 0). y can only become 0 (starts negative, increases by 1: reaches 0, stops). If x is a single-cell run (at two interfaces): x decreases at rate 2: can it cross 0? x = 1: next step: x -= 2 → -1: yes, it crosses! Then the sign flips: the two interfaces: (x_left, x): x_left < 0, x = -1 < 0: same sign: dead. (x, x_right): both < 0: dead. So both interfaces die and x = -1 is frozen. So a single-cell run's cell can end up at -1 (if it crossed) — that's the only "crossing" case. For a run of length ≥ 2: boundary cell x > 0, decreases at rate 1 (only 1 interface): x → 0 exactly (can't go below 0: at x = 0 the interface is dead). So boundary cells of long runs end up ≥ 0 (or 0). Single-cell cells end up at 0 or -1 (if positive) or +1 (if negative and crossed) — or they hit exactly 0.

And: can an interface be "reborn"? No: interfaces die when one side is 0 or when a single cell crosses (both sides become same sign). They never re-form. ✓.
